records.hook: A lake once exploded and killed 1,746 people.
records.openingLine: A lake once exploded and killed 1,746 people.
records.secondBeat: It didn't burst with water. It burst with CO2.
records.scientificMechanism: deep lake water can hold dissolved CO2 under pressure; if it mixes upward, the gas escapes all at once
records.expectedConsequence: a dense gas cloud flows down valleys and suffocates people and animals
records.coreQuestion: If a lake exploded with gas, how could it kill people miles away?
records.misconception: Lake Nyos didn't explode with water or fire; it released a silent, heavy cloud of carbon dioxide.
visualScenes: CO2 bubbles rising from deep water
density comparison of CO2 and air
editorialTitles: The Lake That Suddenly Released a Deadly Cloud
Why Lake Nyos Was So Deadly

facts.claim: On 21 August 1986, a limnic eruption at Lake Nyos in northwestern Cameroon killed 1,746 people and 3,500 livestock.
The eruption triggered the sudden release of about 100,000–300,000 tons of carbon dioxide (CO2).
The supersaturated deep water rapidly mixed with the upper layers of the lake, where the reduced pressure allowed the stored CO2 to effervesce out of solution.
Since carbon dioxide is 50% more dense than air, the cloud hugged the ground and moved down the valleys, where there were various villages.
A degassing system has since been installed at the lake, with the aim of reducing the concentration of CO2 in the waters.

narration.text: A lake once exploded and killed 1,746 people.
It didn't burst with water. It burst with CO2.
Lake Nyos released 100,000 to 300,000 tons of carbon dioxide.
Its deep water was supersaturated, like a shaken soda.
Once mixed upward, the gas fizzed out of solution.
CO2 is 50% denser than air, so the cloud hugged valleys.
Villagers below had no warning and nothing to breathe.
Pipes now vent the gas slowly to prevent a repeat.

records.topic: What If Earth Froze Over Completely?
records.hook: Earth may have frozen to the equator before.
records.openingLine: Earth may have frozen to the equator before.
records.secondBeat: Scientists call it Snowball Earth, over 650 million years ago.
records.scientificMechanism: ice reflects sunlight; past a threshold, spreading ice cools the planet enough to spread further
records.scenarioChange: ice sheets advanced all the way to the equator
records.expectedConsequence: a planet-wide freeze that only volcanic CO2 build-up could eventually break
records.coreQuestion: If Earth froze over completely, how would it ever thaw?
records.misconception: Earth's climate doesn't only have warming tipping points; ice can run away too.
visualScenes: Earth covered in ice to the equator
editorialTitles: When Earth Froze to the Equator
Why Ice Can Run Away on a Planet

facts.claim: The snowball Earth hypothesis postulates that the planet's surface froze more than 650 Ma.
According to modelling, an ice–albedo feedback would result in glacial ice rapidly advancing to the equator once the glaciers spread to within 25° to 30° of the equator.
Palaeomagnetic measurements have indicated that some sediments of glacial origin were deposited within 10 degrees of the equator, although the accuracy of this reconstruction is in question.
A record from Oman covers the period from 712 to 545 million years ago, a time span containing the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations.

narration.text: Earth may have frozen to the equator before.
Scientists call it Snowball Earth, over 650 million years ago.
Ice reflects sunlight, which cools the planet further.
Models show ice runs away once it reaches 25 to 30 degrees of the equator.
Some glacial rocks may have formed within 10 degrees of the equator.
Escaping it would need volcanic CO2 to build up for ages.
Life survived anyway, in pockets we still debate.
So Earth's climate has a freezing tipping point, not just a warming one.

records.topic: What If a Sea Just Disappeared?
records.hook: Why a sea shrank to 25% without a drought.
records.openingLine: Why a sea shrank to 25% without a drought.
records.secondBeat: It was the world's fourth-largest lake in 1960.
records.scientificMechanism: a lake with no outlet stays full only while river inflow matches evaporation
records.scenarioChange: the rivers feeding a large inland sea were diverted
records.expectedConsequence: the sea shrinks, salinity soars and fisheries collapse
records.coreQuestion: If a sea's rivers were diverted, how fast could it disappear?
records.misconception: The Aral Sea didn't dry up from drought; its rivers were diverted for irrigation.
visualScenes: satellite images of the Aral Sea 1960 to 2004
editorialTitles: How the Aral Sea Disappeared
Why a Sea Can Vanish Without a Drought

facts.claim: In 1960, the Aral Sea had been the world's fourth-largest lake with an area of 68,000 km2 (26,000 sq mi) and a volume of 1,100 km3.
In 2004, the sea's surface area was 17,160 km2 (6,630 sq mi), 25% of its original size, and a nearly fivefold increase in salinity had killed most of its flora and fauna.
Large scale construction of irrigation canals first began in the 1930s and was greatly increased in the 1960s.
The North Aral Sea's surface increased from 2,550 square kilometers in 2003 to 3,300 square kilometers in 2008.
By 1988, Uzbekistan was the world's largest exporter of cotton.

narration.text: Why a sea shrank to 25% without a drought.
It was the world's fourth-largest lake in 1960.
It covered 68,000 square kilometres.
Soviet irrigation diverted its rivers to grow cotton.
By 2004, it was down to 17,160 square kilometres.
Salinity rose nearly fivefold, killing most fish and plants.
A dam has since let the North Aral partly recover.
So a sea can vanish without a drought, just by thirst upstream.

records.topic: What If the Amazon Rainforest Disappeared?
records.hook: Why the Amazon isn't really the planet's lungs.
records.openingLine: Why the Amazon isn't really the planet's lungs.
records.secondBeat: The famous quarter-of-oxygen figure is really turnover.
records.scientificMechanism: a mature forest consumes nearly as much oxygen as it produces, but stores vast carbon and biodiversity
records.expectedConsequence: no oxygen crisis, but a large carbon release and mass extinction
records.coreQuestion: If the Amazon disappeared, would we run out of air, or lose something else?
records.misconception: The Amazon doesn't supply a quarter of Earth's oxygen; that figure refers to oxygen turnover.
visualScenes: oxygen in and out balance diagram
map of the Amazon across nine countries
editorialTitles: What Losing the Amazon Would Really Cost
Why the Amazon Isn't the Lungs of the Planet

facts.claim: Though often referenced as producing more than a quarter of the Earth's oxygen, this often stated, but misused statistic actually refers to oxygen turnover.
This basin encompasses 7 million km2 (2.7 million sq mi), of which 6 million km2 (2.3 million sq mi) are covered by the rainforest.
The majority of the forest, 60%, is in Brazil, followed by Peru with 13%, Colombia with 10%.
The region is home to about 2.5 million insect species, tens of thousands of plants, and some 2,000 birds and mammals.

narration.text: Why the Amazon isn't really the planet's lungs.
The famous quarter-of-oxygen figure is really turnover.
The forest covers about 6 million square kilometres.
About 60% of it lies in Brazil.
It holds around 2.5 million insect species.
Losing it wouldn't suffocate us, but it would release huge carbon stores.
It would also erase species found nowhere else.
So the Amazon's real value is carbon and life, not air.

records.topic: What If You Could Feel Neutrinos?
records.hook: 65 billion neutrinos pass through your fingertip every second.
records.openingLine: 65 billion neutrinos pass through your fingertip every second.
records.secondBeat: You never feel them. Almost none ever hit anything.
records.scientificMechanism: neutrinos interact only through the weak force, so almost all pass through matter untouched
records.scenarioChange: neutrinos interacted with matter as strongly as light
records.expectedConsequence: a constant, planet-penetrating glare from the Sun, day and night
records.coreQuestion: If you could feel neutrinos, what would the constant stream through your body be like?
records.misconception: Neutrinos aren't rare; tens of billions cross each square centimetre of you every second.
visualScenes: neutrinos passing through Earth at night
editorialTitles: The Invisible Particles Passing Through You
Why 65 Billion Neutrinos Don't Hurt

facts.claim: Each second, about 65 billion solar neutrinos pass through every square centimeter on the part of the Earth orthogonal to the direction of the Sun.
From calculations based on cosmological models, the sum of the three neutrino masses must be below 0.120 eV/c2.
Koshiba's work resulted in the first real-time observation of neutrinos from the SN 1987A supernova in the nearby Large Magellanic Cloud.
SN 1987A represents the only verified detection of neutrinos from a supernova.

narration.text: 65 billion neutrinos pass through your fingertip every second.
You never feel them. Almost none ever hit anything.
They stream from fusion in the Sun's core.
At night, they pass through Earth and reach you from below.
The three neutrino masses add up to under 0.120 electronvolts.
In 1987, detectors caught neutrinos from a supernova.
If they interacted like light, the Sun would glare through the ground at night.
So one of the most common particles around you goes unnoticed.

records.topic: What If Toilets Really Flushed Backwards Down Under?
records.hook: Why Earth's spin can't steer your toilet.
records.openingLine: Why Earth's spin can't steer your toilet.
records.secondBeat: Identical toilets drain the same way in both hemispheres.
records.scientificMechanism: the Coriolis effect depends on scale and time; in a sink it is swamped by the container's shape and leftover motion
records.scenarioChange: the Coriolis effect controlled household drains
records.expectedConsequence: it doesn't: only carefully stilled tanks, draining slowly, show the effect
records.coreQuestion: If the Coriolis effect ruled your drain, would toilets flush backwards in Australia?
records.misconception: Toilets and sinks don't drain in opposite directions in each hemisphere; the bowl's shape decides.
visualScenes: toilet swirling in both hemispheres side by side
still tank with a floating cross
editorialTitles: Do Toilets Flush Backwards in Australia?
Why Earth's Spin Steers Storms, Not Sinks

facts.claim: Contrary to popular misconception, bathtubs, toilets, and other water receptacles do not drain in opposite directions in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
Identical toilets flushed in both hemispheres drain in the same direction, and this direction is determined mostly by the shape of the toilet bowl.
The theory that the effect determines the rotation of draining water in a household bathtub, sink or toilet has been repeatedly disproven.
In a carefully prepared experiment, it takes 20 minutes to drain, and the cross starts turning only around 15 minutes.

narration.text: Why Earth's spin can't steer your toilet.
Identical toilets drain the same way in both hemispheres.
The bowl's shape sets the swirl, not Earth's spin.
The Coriolis effect is real, but tiny at sink scale.
In one careful test, a still tank took 20 minutes to drain.
Only after about 15 minutes did Earth's rotation show.
At hurricane scale, though, it sets the direction of the spin.
So Earth's rotation steers storms, not your bathroom.

records.topic: What If Lightning Were Hotter Than the Sun?
records.secondBeat: The Sun's surface is only about 5,800 kelvin.
records.scientificMechanism: a lightning channel carries tens of thousands of amperes, heating air almost instantly
records.scenarioChange: you could stand next to a lightning channel
records.expectedConsequence: the air heats beyond the Sun's surface temperature and explodes outward as thunder
records.coreQuestion: Is a lightning bolt really hotter than the surface of the Sun?
records.misconception: Thunder isn't clouds colliding; it's air expanding explosively from lightning's heat.
visualScenes: temperature comparison: lightning versus Sun surface
current flow diagram in a channel
editorialTitles: Why Lightning Is Hotter Than the Sun's Surface
What Makes Thunder

facts.claim: The air around the lightning flash rapidly heats to temperatures of about 30,000 °C (54,000 °F).
An average bolt of negative lightning creates an electric current of 30,000 amperes (30 kA), transferring a total 15 C of electric charge and 1 gigajoule of energy.
Positive lightning is less common than negative lightning and on average makes up less than 5% of all lightning strikes.
The average positive ground flash has roughly double the peak current of a typical negative flash, and can produce peak currents up to 400 kA.
By contrast, the Sun's surface temperature is about 5800 K.

narration.text: Lightning heats air to 30,000 °C.
The Sun's surface is only about 5,800 kelvin.
An average bolt carries 30,000 amperes.
It moves about 1 gigajoule of energy.
Positive lightning is rarer, under 5% of strikes.
But it can peak at 400 kiloamperes.
The heated air explodes outward, and that shockwave is thunder.
So every flash is briefly hotter than the Sun's surface.

records.topic: What If You Jumped From the Edge of Space?
records.hook: Why one skydiver broke the sound barrier.
records.openingLine: Why one skydiver broke the sound barrier.
records.secondBeat: Felix Baumgartner jumped from 38,969 metres up.
records.scientificMechanism: thin air at high altitude creates little drag, so a falling body accelerates far beyond normal terminal velocity
records.scenarioChange: a person jumped from the stratosphere
records.expectedConsequence: a supersonic free fall, survivable only in a pressure suit
records.coreQuestion: If you jumped from the edge of space, how fast would you fall?
records.misconception: Terminal velocity isn't fixed; in thin air, a falling person can break the sound barrier.
editorialTitles: The Man Who Fell Faster Than Sound
Why Thin Air Let a Skydiver Go Supersonic

facts.claim: Reaching 1,357.64 km/h (843.6 mph), Mach 1.25, Baumgartner broke the sound barrier on his descent, becoming the first human being to do so without any form of engine power.
With a final altitude of 38,969 m (127,851 ft; 24 mi), Baumgartner broke the unofficial record for the highest manned balloon flight.
The normal terminal velocity of a skydiver freeflying is about 320 km/h (200 mph or 90 m/s), but the high altitude with less-dense atmosphere would decrease drag.
Baumgartner deployed his parachute after 4 minutes and 19 seconds.

narration.text: Why one skydiver broke the sound barrier.
Felix Baumgartner jumped from 38,969 metres up.
He reached 1,357.64 kilometres per hour, Mach 1.25.
Thin air meant little drag, so he kept accelerating.
A normal skydiver tops out near 320 kilometres per hour.
He opened his parachute after 4 minutes and 19 seconds.
Without a pressure suit, the low pressure would have been fatal.
So the edge of space lets a human outrun sound.

records.topic: What If You Stopped Eating for a Year?
records.hook: One man went 382 days without solid food.
records.openingLine: One man went 382 days without solid food.
records.secondBeat: Angus Barbieri did it under medical supervision.
records.scientificMechanism: during a prolonged fast the body runs mainly on stored fat, which needs medical monitoring to be survivable
records.scenarioChange: a person fasted for over a year under medical supervision
records.expectedConsequence: massive fat loss without ill effects in that case, but only with close supervision
records.coreQuestion: If you stopped eating for a year, could your body survive on its own fat?
records.misconception: Barbieri's fast wasn't unsupervised endurance; doctors monitored him throughout. Don't try it.
editorialTitles: The Man Who Didn't Eat for 382 Days
How a Body Survived a Year Without Food

facts.claim: Angus Barbieri was a Scottish man who fasted for 382 days, from 14 June 1965 to 30 June 1966.
Barbieri went from almost 456 pounds (207 kg) to 180 pounds (82 kg), losing 276 pounds (125 kg) and setting a record for the length of a fast.
Barbieri began his treatment in the hospital but for most of the 382 days lived at home, visiting the hospital for outpatient checkups, including blood and urine samples.
A 1973 study found that Barbieri maintained a healthy weight of 196 pounds (89 kg), concluding that prolonged fasting in this patient had no ill-effects.

narration.text: One man went 382 days without solid food.
Angus Barbieri did it under medical supervision.
He started at 207 kilograms.
He finished at 82, losing 125 kilograms.
His body burned stored fat for energy, day after day.
Doctors checked his blood and urine throughout.
Years later, he had kept a healthy weight of 89 kilograms.
So stored fat can fuel a body for a year, but only with doctors watching.

records.topic: What If You Stayed on Everest's Summit?
records.hook: Above 8,000 metres, your body starts dying.
records.openingLine: Above 8,000 metres, your body starts dying.
records.secondBeat: Climbers call it the death zone.
records.scientificMechanism: oxygen's partial pressure falls with altitude, and above about 8,000 m the body cannot adapt
records.scenarioChange: a climber stayed at the summit instead of descending
records.expectedConsequence: steady deterioration of brain and lungs; survival depends on getting down
records.coreQuestion: If you stayed on Everest's summit, how long could your body cope?
records.misconception: The air at the summit isn't lower in oxygen percentage; its pressure is what drops.
editorialTitles: What the Death Zone Does to Your Body
Why No One Can Live on Everest's Summit

facts.claim: Mountaineers refer to the altitudes above 8,000 metres (26,000 ft) as the death zone, where it is generally believed that no human body can acclimatize.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Effects of high altitude on humans

facts.claim: Oxygen partial pressure is about half of its sea-level value at 5,000 m, the altitude of the Everest Base Camp, and only a third at 8,848 m, the summit of Mount Everest.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Effects of high altitude on humans

facts.claim: After the human body reaches around 2,100 metres (6,900 ft) above sea level, the saturation of oxyhemoglobin begins to decrease rapidly.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Effects of high altitude on humans

facts.claim: The concentration of oxygen (O2) in sea-level air is 20.9%, so the partial pressure of O2 is 21.136 kilopascals.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Effects of high altitude on humans

narration.text: Above 8,000 metres, your body starts dying.
Climbers call it the death zone.
No human body can acclimatize up there.
On Everest's summit, oxygen pressure is a third of sea level's.
Even at base camp, 5,000 metres up, it's about half.
Blood oxygen starts dropping sharply above 2,100 metres.
Stay too long, and brain and lungs begin to fail.
So Everest's summit is a place you visit, never a place you stay.

records.topic: What If You Lived on Mars?
records.hook: Why Mars's 38% gravity is the easy part.
records.openingLine: Why Mars's 38% gravity is the easy part.
records.secondBeat: The air there is 0.6% of Earth's pressure.
records.scientificMechanism: Mars's thin atmosphere and lack of a global magnetic field leave its surface cold, low-pressure and exposed to radiation
records.scenarioChange: people settled on the Martian surface
records.expectedConsequence: every habitat needs pressure, shielding and soil treatment to keep people alive
records.coreQuestion: If you lived on Mars, what would be harder: the low gravity or everything else?
records.misconception: Mars's gravity isn't the main problem; the thin air, radiation and toxic soil are.
editorialTitles: What Living on Mars Would Really Be Like
Why Mars's Gravity Is the Easy Part

facts.claim: Mars has about 15% of Earth's volume and 11% of Earth's mass, resulting in about 38% of Earth's surface gravity.
The resulting mean surface pressure is only 0.6% of Earth's 101.3 kPa (14.69 psi).
At the average surface level the atmospheric temperature ranges from −153 to 20 °C, and cosmic radiation is high.
The Martian soil has a basic pH of 7.7, and contains 0.6% perchlorate by weight, concentrations that are toxic to humans.

narration.text: Why Mars's 38% gravity is the easy part.
The air there is 0.6% of Earth's pressure.
Mars has 11% of Earth's mass.
Temperatures swing from −153 to 20 °C.
Its soil holds 0.6% perchlorate, toxic to humans.
Cosmic radiation at the surface is high.
So every Martian home would need pressure, shielding and filters.
So on Mars, the hard part is simply staying alive.

records.topic: What If We Swam in Europa's Ocean?
records.hook: Europa hides more water than all Earth's oceans.
records.openingLine: Europa hides more water than all Earth's oceans.
records.secondBeat: It's under an icy shell on a moon of Jupiter.
records.scientificMechanism: tidal flexing by Jupiter keeps a salty ocean liquid beneath Europa's ice shell
records.expectedConsequence: a vast, dark ocean that could host life, reachable only through ice
records.coreQuestion: If we swam in Europa's ocean, what would we find under the ice?
records.misconception: Earth isn't the water world of the Solar System; Europa may hold more water than all our oceans.
visualScenes: cutaway of ice shell and ocean
editorialTitles: The Hidden Ocean on Jupiter's Moon
Why Europa Has More Water Than Earth

facts.claim: This leads to a volume of Europa's oceans of 3×1018m3, between two or three times the volume of Earth's oceans.
Models suggest the outer elastic portion of the ice crust could be as thin as 200 metres (660 ft).
In May 2018, astronomers provided supporting evidence of water plume activity on Europa, based on data from the Galileo space probe.
In September 2022, the Juno spacecraft flew within around 320km (200 miles) of Europa.

narration.text: Europa hides more water than all Earth's oceans.
It's under an icy shell on a moon of Jupiter.
Its ocean may be 2 to 3 times Earth's ocean volume.
The rigid top layer of ice may be as thin as 200 metres.
Plumes of water may erupt through cracks.
In 2022, Juno flew within 320 kilometres of it.
Reaching the water would still mean drilling through ice.
So the best place to look for life may be under ice, not on land.

records.topic: What If We Sent a Probe to Another Star?
records.hook: Why a star probe needs 100 gigawatts of lasers.
records.openingLine: Why a star probe needs 100 gigawatts of lasers.
records.secondBeat: Its sail must reach a fifth of light speed.
records.scientificMechanism: ground-based lasers push a gram-scale probe on an ultra-thin light sail to a large fraction of light speed
records.scenarioChange: humanity launched a laser-driven probe toward Alpha Centauri
records.expectedConsequence: a decades-long flight needing enormous lasers, survivable sails and huge funding
records.coreQuestion: If we sent a probe to another star, what would it take to get there within a lifetime?
records.misconception: The hard part isn't the probe; it's a 100-gigawatt laser array and surviving interstellar dust.
visualScenes: light sail catching a laser beam
editorialTitles: What It Would Take to Reach Another Star
Why Interstellar Probes Need 100-Gigawatt Lasers

facts.claim: The probes would be propelled by a square-kilometre array of 10 kW ground-based lasers with a combined output of up to 100 GW.
To accelerate the 4 m sail at 10,000 Gs to 0.2 c requires combining optics which are approximately 3 kilometers in diameter.
The spacecraft will have to survive collisions with space dust; each square centimeter of frontal cross-section is expected to collide with about a thousand particles of size at least 0.1 μm.
Milner placed the final mission cost at $5–10 billion.
In September 2025, Scientific American reported that the project was on hold indefinitely.

narration.text: Why a star probe needs 100 gigawatts of lasers.
Its sail must reach a fifth of light speed.
The probes would weigh grams, on ultra-thin sails.
Focusing that beam needs optics about 3 kilometres across.
Every square centimetre would hit about a thousand dust grains.
Estimates put the mission at $5 to 10 billion.
In 2025, the project was reported on hold indefinitely.
So reaching another star is possible on paper, and very hard in practice.

records.topic: What If We Sucked Carbon Out of the Air?
records.hook: Why 36,000 tonnes a year barely dents CO2.
records.openingLine: Why 36,000 tonnes a year barely dents CO2.
records.secondBeat: That's the capacity of the biggest air-capture plant.
records.scientificMechanism: direct air capture pulls CO2 from ambient air with sorbents, then releases it for storage using energy
records.scenarioChange: direct air capture scaled up to climate-relevant size
records.expectedConsequence: enormous numbers of plants, energy and water would be needed; cost remains the barrier
records.coreQuestion: If we sucked carbon out of the air, how big would the machines need to be?
records.misconception: Air capture isn't a substitute for cutting emissions; today's largest plant handles tiny amounts.
visualScenes: scale gap chart: plant versus need
editorialTitles: Can We Vacuum Carbon Out of the Sky?
Why Air Capture Can't Replace Emission Cuts

facts.claim: The current largest DAC plant, Climeworks Mammoth, has a capacity of just 36,000 tonnes CO2 per annum with a capture cost of $1,000 (£774) per tCO2.
The IEA estimates that capture of at least 85 million tonnes and 980 million tonnes of CO2 annually by 2030 and 2050, respectively, are needed to achieve net zero.
The actual performance has averaged 600 tonnes per year since it started operating, and fails to even extract sufficient CO2 to compensate for its own emissions.
It was estimated that to capture 3.3 gigatonnes of CO2 a year would require 300 km3 of water, or 4% of the water used for irrigation.

narration.text: Why 36,000 tonnes a year barely dents CO2.
That's the capacity of the biggest air-capture plant.
Capture there costs about $1,000 per tonne.
Net zero may need 980 million tonnes a year by 2050.
That's tens of thousands of plants like it.
An earlier plant, Orca, averaged just 600 tonnes a year.
It didn't even offset its own emissions.
So air capture helps at the edges. Cutting emissions does the heavy lifting.

records.topic: What If Two Neutron Stars Collided?
records.hook: One crash forged 10 Earths of gold and platinum.
records.openingLine: One crash forged 10 Earths of gold and platinum.
records.scientificMechanism: merging neutron stars eject neutron-rich matter where rapid neutron capture builds heavy elements
records.scenarioChange: two neutron stars spiralled together and merged
records.expectedConsequence: gravitational waves, a gamma-ray burst and a kilonova forging gold and platinum
records.coreQuestion: If two neutron stars collided, what would the crash create?
records.misconception: Gold isn't made in ordinary stars; much of it comes from collisions like this.
visualScenes: periodic table with heavy elements highlighted
editorialTitles: The Collision That Made Gold
Where Your Gold Really Came From

facts.claim: GW170817 was a gravitational wave observed by the LIGO and Virgo detectors on 17 August 2017, originating within the galaxy NGC 4993, about 140 million light years away.
GW170817 had an audible duration of approximately 100 seconds and exhibited the characteristic intensity and frequency expected of the inspiral of two neutron stars.
A short gamma-ray burst of around 2 seconds was detected by the Fermi and INTEGRAL spacecraft beginning 1.7 seconds after the GW emitted by the merger.
A total of 16,000 times the mass of the Earth in heavy elements is believed to have formed, including approximately 10 Earth masses just of the two elements gold and platinum.

narration.text: One crash forged 10 Earths of gold and platinum.
LIGO heard it on 17 August 2017.
The collision was about 140 million light-years away.
Its gravitational-wave signal lasted about 100 seconds.
1.7 seconds later, a gamma-ray burst arrived.
In total, 16,000 Earth masses of heavy elements formed.
Some of the gold on Earth likely came from events like this.
So your jewellery may be debris from a stellar collision.

records.topic: What If Earth Were Squeezed Into a Black Hole?
records.hook: Earth would become a black hole at 9 millimetres.
records.openingLine: Earth would become a black hole at 9 millimetres.
records.secondBeat: That's its Schwarzschild radius, about a marble's size.
records.scientificMechanism: any mass compressed inside its Schwarzschild radius becomes a black hole; its gravity far away stays the same
records.scenarioChange: Earth was compressed to its Schwarzschild radius
records.expectedConsequence: a marble-sized black hole the Moon would keep orbiting unchanged
records.coreQuestion: If Earth were squeezed into a black hole, what would change for the Moon?
records.misconception: Black holes don't suck everything in; at the same mass, their pull far away is unchanged.
visualScenes: Moon orbiting a tiny black hole
gravity field lines unchanged at distance
Sun as a 3 km black hole
editorialTitles: What If Earth Became a Black Hole
Why Black Holes Aren't Cosmic Vacuum Cleaners

facts.claim: The Sun has a Schwarzschild radius of approximately 3.0 km (1.9 mi), whereas Earth's is approximately 9 mm (0.35 in) and the Moon's is approximately 0.1 mm (0.004 in).
The Schwarzschild radius was named after the German astronomer Karl Schwarzschild, who calculated this solution for the theory of general relativity in 1916.
Supermassive black holes up to 21 billion solar masses have been detected, such as NGC 4889.
Supermassive black holes, unlike stellar mass black holes, have comparatively low average densities.

narration.text: Earth would become a black hole at 9 millimetres.
That's its Schwarzschild radius, about a marble's size.
The Sun's is about 3 kilometres.
The Moon's is just 0.1 millimetres.
From far away, the same mass pulls just as hard.
The Moon would keep orbiting exactly as before.
But we'd have no ground left to stand on.
So a black hole isn't a cosmic vacuum cleaner. It's just dense.

records.hook: Why 1% of plant life makes half our oxygen.
records.openingLine: Why 1% of plant life makes half our oxygen.
records.secondBeat: Those are phytoplankton, tiny drifting ocean plants.
records.scientificMechanism: phytoplankton photosynthesise at the base of marine food webs, producing oxygen and fixing carbon
records.expectedConsequence: marine food webs collapse from the bottom; oxygen reserves last, but ocean life does not
records.coreQuestion: If ocean plankton disappeared, what would run out first: air or fish?
records.misconception: Losing plankton wouldn't make us suffocate quickly; the atmosphere's oxygen reserve is huge. Food webs would collapse first.
visualScenes: energy lost at each trophic level
editorialTitles: What If the Ocean's Plankton Vanished
Why the Smallest Ocean Life Holds Up the Largest

facts.claim: Phytoplankton account for about half of global photosynthetic activity and at least half of the oxygen production, despite amounting to only about 1% of the global plant biomass.
Approximately 90% of total carbon is lost between trophic levels due to respiration, detritus, and dissolved organic matter.
Redfield proposed that the ratio of carbon to nitrogen to phosphorus (106:16:1) in the ocean was controlled by the phytoplankton's requirements.
Some scientists advocate iron fertilization as a means to counteract the accumulation of human-produced carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

narration.text: Why 1% of plant life makes half our oxygen.
Those are phytoplankton, tiny drifting ocean plants.
They do about half of Earth's photosynthesis.
They sit at the base of nearly every marine food web.
About 90% of carbon is lost at each step up the food chain.
Without them, fish stocks would collapse from the bottom up.
The air wouldn't run out fast, but ocean life would.
So the ocean's smallest organisms hold up its largest.

facts.claim: The Haber process enabled the global population to increase from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by November 2018.
Although atmospheric nitrogen (N2) is abundant, comprising ~78% of the air, it is exceptionally stable and does not readily react with other chemicals.
On each pass, only about 15% conversion occurs; due to the recycling of leftover reactants, eventually conversion of 97% is achieved.
The Haber process consumes 3–5% of the world's natural gas production (around 1–2% of the world's energy supply).

narration.text: Why 7.7 billion people depend on air-made fertilizer.
The Haber process pulls nitrogen from the air.
Air is about 78% nitrogen, but it barely reacts.
Each pass converts only about 15% into ammonia.
Recycling the gases eventually reaches 97% conversion.
It uses 3 to 5% of the world's natural gas.
Without it, today's harvests couldn't feed today's population.
So much of the food on your plate began as air.
